source.title: Forget Sharpness: Perturbed Forgetting of Model Biases Within SAM Dynamics
source.authors: Ankit Vani; Frederick Tung; Gabriel L. Oliveira; Hossein Sharifi-Noghabi

page_placements.theme: Curvature and flatness are conditional generalization correlates

record.file_problem: The supplied paper text appears complete; no garbling or truncation affecting the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how a forgetting quantity and sharpness correlate with generalization, and reports models with better accuracy despite higher sharpness. This refines the claim that sharpness tracks generalization; its other experiments test a new SAM perturbation rather than the catalog's listed interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper's OBF-versus-steepest-ascent accuracy results test a newly proposed training method, so they are not rows. The CIFAR-10 forgetting-versus-accuracy correlation in Figure 2 is a result on a measured property named in V7. No result tests V1–V6 or V8. Cited findings in the related work are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study tests relationships involving Hessian dominant-eigenvalue sharpness, output-information forgetting, and test accuracy. These do not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus training–test gaps. Its results therefore bear on a broader sharpness hypothesis, but none of the specified versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors propose perturbed forgetting as an alternative explanation of SAM, report settings where it correlates with accuracy more strongly than Hessian-based flatness, and show that OBF can improve accuracy while producing sharper solutions. They do not establish that magnitude-aware sharpness fails to rank generalization gaps.
record.recipe_differences: Measures output-information forgetting and Hessian dominant-eigenvalue sharpness during SAM training, and introduces OBF perturbations; it does not reproduce the magnitude-aware perturbation-tolerance measurement in V7.
record.method_sensitivity: The forgetting–accuracy correlation is plotted across adjusted binning thresholds and three perturbation types. OBF effects vary by architecture; the paper says ViTs benefit more than ResNets and the best γ differs by architecture. For the reported ImageNet baselines, SAM and GSAM schedule ρ, while OBF keeps ρ constant.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2 reports adjusted thresholds where output-information forgetting correlates with final CIFAR-10 accuracy more strongly than Hessian-based flatness; exact sharpness correlations are unreadable in the supplied text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Perturbation-induced forgetting can correlate with held-out accuracy more strongly than Hessian-based flatness in SAM-trained vision transformers.

fits_no_version.finding: On ImageNet, SAM with OBF raises ViT-S/16 accuracy from 78.73% to 80.30% while raising the dominant Hessian eigenvalue from 2.4 to 17.1. ResNet-101 also shows increases in both quantities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher held-out accuracy under a changed SAM perturbation need not coincide with a lower dominant Hessian eigenvalue.

fits_no_version.finding: OBF improves ImageNet accuracy with lower mean Hessian sharpness for ViT-S/32 and ResNet-50, whereas the other recorded architectures show higher mean sharpness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relationship between changes in Hessian sharpness and accuracy under OBF depends on architecture.

record.problems: Figure 2 provides no exact correlation values in the supplied text; the tested sharpness is the Hessian dominant eigenvalue, not magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance. The ImageNet OBF comparisons change the training method, so they are not direct within-recipe correlations between sharpness and the training–test gap. The paper is limited to image classification experiments.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were omitted. Table 1 ImageNet robustness and transfer results compare the newly proposed OBF training method with other methods and do not directly measure V7's specified sharpness–gap relationship.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting capacity and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning. Different base optimizers are used for different architectures without a controlled optimizer comparison.
Training batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations. Perturbation batch size is distinct from the update batch size.
Effects of adding or removing dropout.

Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance ranking training–test gaps among convolutional networks at similarly low training loss, including comparison with norm- and margin-based measures. Hessian eigenvalue comparisons do not test this version.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Remove both proposed V7 limits_scope labels. Measuring a different sharpness construct is an untested portion of V7, not evidence limiting its scope. Appendix B's ASAM comparisons also evaluate Hessian sharpness, despite ASAM using adaptive perturbations, so they do not supply a missing V7 test.

versions.untested_parts: Whether architectures that fit random labels generalize on natural labels.
Whether widening beyond interpolation continues to lower test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning or training recipes.
Large-batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets.

The paper measures sharpness and correlates it with accuracy, but does not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or compare the listed norm- and margin-based measures. The correlation is shown for CIFAR-10 models trained with different SAM perturbations.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.
